Before inspecting the project, parse the complete /brag invocation. If the invocation contains --voice, set voice.enabled = true. Enable narration only for that run. Do not enable narration automatically and do not fall back to the normal no-voice workflow.

/brag turns the current project website or app into a short, polished, shareable launch video using Hyperframes. It is narrow, opinionated, and fun.

What this skill does

  1. Reads the current project code to understand the app.
  2. Plans a short brag concept specific to this project.
  3. Scripts and storyboards the video.
  4. Hands a focused composition brief to Hyperframes.
  5. Validates, renders, and writes share copy.

Parsing the invocation

The user may invoke with natural language or flags:

/brag
/brag --tone chaotic
/brag --tone polished --format vertical
/brag this. Make it feel like a ridiculous startup launch.

Parse these options:

Option Values Default
--tone preset or freeform description inferred
--format landscape, vertical, square landscape
--duration seconds auto (15-25s)
--no-music flag music on
--no-sfx flag sfx on
--title string inferred from project
--voice flag narration off

Voice is opt-in. If --voice is present, use Kokoro via Hyperframes and do not add any provider-selection logic. The voice workflow is intentionally single-provider.

Tone can be a preset (default, polished, yc-parody, chaotic, deadpan, cinematic, app-store) or a creative direction such as "fake Series A launch from 2016", "museum exhibit", or "overproduced mobile game ad".

When the user gives freeform tone direction, map it to the nearest preset for pacing and structure, but preserve the user's direction in the plan and composition brief.

Narration guidance

When --voice is enabled, write narration that complements the visuals, does not simply read visible text, matches scene pacing, sounds natural and conversational, and moves smoothly between scenes. Keep the script concise and specific to the product so the voice feels like part of the edit rather than a separate narration track.

Output directory

By default, output goes to brag-output/. To avoid overwriting previous runs, use a timestamped directory:

brag-output-2026-05-04-143022/

Use a timestamp when: - The user explicitly asks for a new run without overriding previous results - A brag-output/ directory already exists in the project

Generate the timestamp at the start of the run (YYYY-MM-DD-HHmmss) and use it consistently for all output paths in that run: plan, brief, composition, render, and share copy.

Skill directory

<skill-dir> is the directory containing this SKILL.md. Claude Code prints it as "Base directory for this skill" when the skill loads; for other agents it's wherever the skill was installed. Bundled assets are under <skill-dir>/assets/ and scripts under <skill-dir>/scripts/. Don't guess an install path: a plugin install, a ~/.claude/skills/ copy, and this repo all put it somewhere different.

Tone system

Seven tone presets ship with /brag. Each changes scripting energy, pacing, typography personality, and transition style. Presets are defaults, not limits.

Full definitions: references/tones.md

Tone Energy One-liner
default Playful, clean, postable The good-vibes default
polished Serious, elegant For projects that are not jokes
yc-parody Deadpan startup energy Fake seriousness applied to absurd projects
chaotic Fast, loud, aggressive Over-the-top and unhinged
deadpan Calm, dry, understated The joke is that nothing is a joke
cinematic Dramatic, trailer-scale Big motion, bigger claims
app-store Smooth, feature-card clean Corporate but not boring

Always allow a freeform creative direction to refine or override the preset.

Creative laws

These apply to every brag video regardless of tone.

Short. 15–25 seconds. Not one second more without a reason. This holds whether or not narration is on; narration does not extend the window.

Readable. Keep the pace high through motion and cuts, never by flashing text. Every line a viewer must read holds long enough to read it (short label ~0.8s settled; a sentence ~0.3s per word). Fast-in, then hold — never fast-in, then gone.

Specific. The video must feel like it was made for this exact project, not any project.

Show the thing. At least one scene must display actual UI, copy, or a key visual from the product. No abstract filler.

No generic SaaS language. "Streamline your workflow" is banned. Use the project's actual copy and claims.

The hook is everything. The first 2 seconds determine whether someone keeps watching. Plan the hook before anything else.

Funny earns its place. Humor should come from the project's absurdity, not from trying to be funny.

Pattern:

Hook (2-3s) → Reveal (2-4s) → 2-3 sharp highlights (5-12s) → Punchline/outro (2-4s)

Adapt this. Not every project needs exactly 3 highlights. The pattern is a starting shape, not a template.

2	
3	Read the project directory to understand what you're bragging about.
4	
5	## What to look for
6	
7	Read these in priority order:
8	
9	1. **`index.html`** — the primary source. Read the full file. Extract: page title, hero headline, tagline, all section headings, CTA text, testimonial copy, nav items. This is the voice and story of the app.
10	
11	2. **`styles.css`** or equivalent — extract: primary color palette (look for CSS custom properties / `:root` vars), font families, background colors, accent colors. These become the visual identity of the brag video.
12	
13	3. **`README.md`** — if present, extract: project name, one-line description, any listed features.
14	
15	4. **`package.json`** — if present, extract: `name`, `description`.
16	
17	5. **Subdirectory files** — if this is a multi-page app, scan route files, component files, or page files. Extract key feature names and screen descriptions.
18	
19	6. **The user flow / happy path** — scan beyond marketing pages. The brag's strongest material is usually the product *in use*, not the product's marketing of itself. Look at:
20	   - **Routes** (`app/`, `pages/`, route files) — the screens beyond the landing page.
21	   - **Key feature components** — the upload form, the editor, the result view, the dashboard.
22	   - **State machines, stores, or step components** — how a session progresses.
23	   - **README "how it works" or "usage" sections** — the project's own description of the flow.
24	   - **Example or demo folders** — sample inputs and outputs the team tested with.
25	
26	   Identify the 2–3 beats of *using* the product: **entry → key action → result.**
27	
28	7. **`public/` or `assets/`** — note any images, logos, icons. These can be referenced in the composition.
29	
30	## The 9-question rubric
31	
32	After reading, answer all nine. Write these down before moving to Step 2.
33	
34	```
35	1. What is the app?
36	   One sentence. What does it actually do (or claim to do)?
37	
38	2. What is the funniest or most impressive claim?
39	   The one line from the site that earns a reaction.
40	
41	3. What is the visual hook?
42	   The strongest CSS visual: a color palette moment, a UI element, a diagram, a card.
43	
44	4. What should be shown from the actual UI?
45	   Which section of the site has the most video-worthy content?
46	   (Hero? Feature section? Testimonial? The UI mockup?)
47	
48	5. What is the shortest satisfying video?
49	   Would 15 seconds work? 20? What's the minimum to land the joke/claim?
50	
51	6. What tone fits best?
52	   If the user specified a preset, use it.
53	   If the user gave freeform direction, preserve it and map it to the nearest preset.
54	   If the user did not specify, infer both:
55	   - Tone preset: one of the known presets
56	   - Creative direction: a short custom phrase for this project
57	   Examples:
58	   - Absurd product → preset: yc-parody; direction: fake startup launch
59	   - Earnest product → preset: polished; direction: quiet premium product film
60	   - Chaotic product → preset: chaotic; direction: overproduced social ad
61	
62	7. What should the audio feel like?
63	   Decide the audio role and music direction before picking exact SFX files.
64	   Bias toward a polished audio layer: include music and tasteful SFX unless
65	   the user disabled them, assets are missing, or silence is clearly the
66	   strongest creative choice.
67	   Examples:
68	   - Warm corporate bed; SFX chosen later to match real UI motion
69	   - Low music bed with final fade; one dry logo hit if the composition supports it
70	   - Dense chaotic music; Hyperframes may align text/card reveals to beats
71	   - Cinematic bed with a low swell, restrained motion-matched accents, and subtle audio-reactive glow/presence if it supports the visual style
72	
73	8. What should the share caption say?
74	   Draft one sentence. This becomes share-copy.txt.
75	
76	9. What's the user flow worth showing?
77	   The 2–3 beats a real user goes through: entry → key action → result.
78	   Not the landing page's section list — the working app.
79	   Examples:
80	   - Upload long video → see it processing with progress → see 3 vertical clips ready
81	   - Type a message → assistant types back → user clicks "mark resolved"
82	   - Swipe right on Thunder's profile → match animation → chat opens
83	   If the project is a landing-page-only static site with no app, write
84	   "none — landing-page only" and rely on the strongest visual (Q3) instead.
85	```
86	
87	## Color extraction
88	
89	When reading CSS, look for custom properties like:
90	
91	```css
92	:root {
93	  --primary: oklch(...);
94	  --bg: oklch(...);
95	  --accent: ...;
96	}
97	```
98	
99	If no custom properties exist, scan for the most-used colors in background, color, and border rules.
100	
101	Write down:
102	- Background color (exact value)
103	- Primary text color
104	- Accent/brand color
105	- Any gradient or special treatment
106	
107	These colors are recorded in `composition-brief.md` and carry into the composition's look (see the `hyperframes` skill's `references/look.md`).
108	
109	## Font extraction
110	
111	Look for:
112	- `font-family` declarations in `:root` or `body`
113	- Google Fonts `<link>` in `<head>` (the font families are in the URL query string)
114	- `@import` statements
115	
116	Write down the display font (used for headings) and the body font separately.
117	
118	## What to skip
119	
120	Don't read:
121	- Generated build artifacts (`dist/`, `.next/`, `build/`)
122	- Lock files (`package-lock.json`, `yarn.lock`)
123	- Test files
124	- `.git/`
125	- Environment and secret files (`.env`, `.env.*`)
126	- Credential and key material (`.pem`, `.key`, `id_rsa`, service-account JSON, anything under a `secrets/` or `credentials/` directory)
127	- Local config that commonly holds tokens
128	- Any file the project's `.gitignore` excludes for the reasons above
129	
130	## Rule: nothing secret leaves this step
131	
132	Everything read in this step can end up on screen in a video the user posts publicly. Never carry secrets, API keys, tokens, internal hostnames or URLs, real customer or user names, email addresses, or any personal data into `brag-plan.md`, `composition-brief.md`, the composition, the rendered video, or share copy. If the product's real UI contains such data, substitute plausible fictional stand-ins and say so in the plan.

1	# Step 2: Write the brag plan
2	
3	Write `<output-dir>/brag-plan.md`. One focused page. This is the creative north star for the entire video.
4	
5	The plan should specify what the video must communicate and what project material must be used. It should not prescribe low-level Hyperframes implementation details. Hyperframes will decide the concrete composition structure, animation mechanics, and render workflow from the brief in Step 3.
6	
7	## Create the output directory
8	
9	```bash
10	mkdir -p <output-dir>
11	```
12	
13	## Structure of brag-plan.md
14	
15	```markdown

17	
18	## What is this app?
19	[One sentence. What it does, what makes it funny or impressive.]
20	
21	## The angle
22	[The creative premise. The joke, the hook, the claim.
23	What makes this video specific to this project and not generic.]
24	
25	## Hook (first 2-3 seconds)
26	[The opening moment. This is the most important decision.
27	What word, image, or motion earns the next 20 seconds?]
28	
29	## Key moments (the middle)
30	[2-3 sharp highlights from the product.
31	Bullet points. Specific. "The altitude meter counting up." 
32	Not "feature callouts."]
33	
34	## Outro / punchline
35	[How does it land? The final line. The beat before the logo.]
36	
37	## User flow worth showing
38	[The 2–3 beats of *using* the product (entry → key action → result), pulled from
39	Step 1 question 9. This is the strongest material the video has — the centerpiece
40	scenes should show the flow, not just landing-page sections. If the project is
41	landing-page-only, write "none — landing-page only" and rely on Key moments instead.]
42	
43	## Tone
44	- Preset: [default / polished / yc-parody / chaotic / deadpan / cinematic / app-store]
45	- Creative direction: [freeform phrase, inferred or user-provided]
46	- Interpretation: [one sentence on how this affects pacing, writing, visual energy, and restraint]
47	
48	## Format: [landscape / vertical / square] — [width]x[height]
49	## Duration: [target seconds]
50	
51	## Visual identity (from the project)
52	- Background: [exact color value]
53	- Accent: [exact color value]
54	- Text: [exact color value]
55	- Display font: [name]
56	- Body font: [name]
57	- Strongest visual element: [what from the site to reference]
58	
59	## Share copy (draft)
60	[One sentence for Twitter/X/LinkedIn/Discord. Punchy. Not corporate.]
61	
62	## Audio direction
63	- Role: [warm bed / sparse professional accents / cinematic support / dense rhythmic layer / intentional silence]
64	- Music: [candidate track / mood / none only if disabled, missing, or intentionally silent]
65	- Music treatment: [start time, volume posture, fade-in/out intent, beat/swell notes]
66	- Music cue guidance: [preset cue file read / unavailable; list 1-3 strongCue timestamps for major moments; list beat-grid windows for sequential events]
67	- Audio-reactive treatment: [none / subtle / expressive; what visual qualities may respond to music energy]
68	- SFX posture: [sparse / moderate / dense; motion-matched; professional restraint]
69	- Audio-coupled moments: [visual ideas that should consider sound, e.g. typed text, beat reveal, count-up, card sequence]
70	- Restraint rule: [what audio must not do]
71	
72	## Storyboard
73

75	[What's on screen. What text appears. What product material must be referenced.]
76	Sequential/interaction: [yes — describe what appears one by one or what interaction is simulated, e.g. "3 stat cards arrive one by one" or "cursor clicks the match button"; or none]

83	[...]
84	Sequential/interaction: [yes — describe it; or none]
85	Audio intent: [what the sound should do emotionally]
86	Audio-coupled idea: [type or none]
87	Transition mood: [mood] → Scene 3
88	
89	[... continue for all scenes]
90

92	**Audio summary:** [one sentence describing the full audio arc]
93	```
94	
95	## Planning the scenes
96	
97	The default pattern is:
98	```
99	Hook → Reveal → 2-3 highlights → Punchline/outro
100	```
101	
102	But adapt it. These are the right scene counts for each tone:
103	
104	| Tone | Scenes | Pacing |
105	|---|---|---|
106	| `default` | 4-5 | Comfortable. Room for each moment to breathe. |
107	| `polished` | 3-4 | Fewer scenes, longer holds. Confidence through restraint. |
108	| `yc-parody` | 4-5 | Structured. The joke is how seriously it's delivered. |
109	| `chaotic` | 6-8 | Rapid. Some scenes under 2 seconds. |
110	| `deadpan` | 3-4 | Long holds. Big empty space. One word at a time. |
111	| `cinematic` | 4-5 | Wide shots. Big type. Dramatic reveals. |
112	| `app-store` | 4-6 | Feature cards. Clean reveals. No mess. |
113	
114	## Duration guidance
115	
116	Scene durations must sum to 15-25 seconds. Count them.
117	
118	- Under 15 seconds: too thin, add a scene or lengthen holds.
119	- Over 25 seconds: cut a scene or tighten timing.
120	- 18-22 seconds is the sweet spot for most brag videos.
121	
122	## Reading time (keep the pace, not at text's expense)
123	
124	High pace comes from fast motion, fast transitions, and tight cuts — NOT from pulling text off screen before it can be read. Every text element a viewer must read needs enough fully-visible, settled time (entered, not yet exiting) to actually read it:
125	
126	- Short label or 1-3 word line: about 0.8s settled.
127	- Headline or full sentence: about 0.3s per word, minimum ~1.2s. The hook line gets the most.
128	
129	Plan that floor, then keep everything else fast: entrances and transitions stay snappy (0.3-0.6s) and motion stays energetic. A line can SLAM in fast and then HOLD — fast-in plus an adequate hold reads as punchy AND legible.
130	
131	Two failure modes to design out at the plan stage:
132	
133	- **Too much text for the scene length.** A 4s scene lands maybe 2-3 short reads at the floor, not 6. If a scene carries more text than its duration allows, cut copy or split the scene — do not speed it up.
134	- **Sequential text snapped onto a fast beat.** Beat-grid reveals can land ~0.5s apart at 110+ BPM (this is what rushed the bicycles spec rows). That spacing is fine for accents (glows, dots, ticks) but too fast for readable lines. For sequential TEXT, hold each item to the floor: snap to every other beat, or reveal them quickly and hold the full set on screen afterward. Flag any sequential text reveal in the storyboard with its intended hold.
135	
136	## Choosing what to show
137	
138	Every brag video must show something real from the product. Options, in preferred order:
139	
140	1. **Recreate a working-app moment** — the upload screen, the result view, the dashboard with real-looking content. Use real source from `app/`, `pages/`, or routed components — not just the landing page. This is the most compelling option whenever the product has a flow. The product *doing* its thing beats the product *describing* its thing.
141	2. **Recreate a UI element in HTML** — a hero card, swipe UI, progress meter, stat block. Strong when there is no flow to show.
142	3. **Animate the core concept** — if the product is "taxis for taxis", animate two taxis where one is in the other. Pure graphic but grounded in the idea.
143	4. **Text-forward sequence** — if the product is copy-driven (Psychologists for Chatbots), let the copy be the visual. Giant display type, minimal chrome.
144	
145	Never fill scenes with abstract patterns, color washes, or generic motion graphics that could belong to any video.
146	
147	## Bias the storyboard toward the user flow
148	
149	If Step 1 question 9 identified a real user flow, the **centerpiece scenes must show that flow** — not just landing-page recreations.
150	
151	Good (working-app scenes):
152	- "Upload screen — cursor drops a video file. Filename appears. Progress bar fills 0→100% in 1.2s."
153	- "Three result thumbnails pop in: 0:15, 0:23, 0:31. Each shows a vertical clip frame with a real-looking caption."
154	- "Inbox row appears, gets a green 'resolved' badge, slides off the top of the list."
155	
156	Avoid (marketing-only scenes when a flow exists):
157	- "16:9 → 9:16 transform diagram" — that's a *diagram of what the product does*, not the product doing it.
158	- "Three stat cards: 10x faster / 0 cuts / 3 clips" — that's the landing page's social-proof row, not the product.
159	
160	Stat cards, headline blocks, and the landing-page hero still have a place — but at most one of them, used as a frame around the flow, not as a substitute. The centerpiece is the working app.
161	
162	If the project has no app (landing-page-only static site), skip this section and recreate the landing-page strongest visual instead.
163	
164	## Look for interaction and sequential reveal moments
165	
166	Before writing the storyboard, ask: **does this product have things that can appear one by one, or actions that can be simulated?**
167	
168	These are among the most effective moments in a brag video — they make the product feel alive and real, not like a slide deck. Look for:
169	
170	- **Sequential reveals** — feature cards, stats, list items, match results, profile cards, menu options, or anything the product shows as a set. Design these to appear one by one so sound and motion reinforce each arrival. This is a storyboard decision, not an audio afterthought.
171	- **Simulated interaction** — if the product involves swiping, clicking, typing, selecting, or toggling, show it. A cursor clicking a button, a swipe gesture on a card, or text being typed into a field turns a static mockup into a demonstration. Sound matches the action automatically when the gesture is in the storyboard.
172	
173	If a scene has either of these, commit to it explicitly in the scene description:
174	- Good: "3 horse profiles slide in one by one, each with a card sound"
175	- Good: "Simulate a right-swipe on Thunder's profile card"
176	- Good: "The hook line types out character by character with keyboard sounds"
177	- Avoid: leaving it vague and hoping Hyperframes adds rhythm on its own
178	
179	Hyperframes can implement both patterns well — but only if the plan specifies what's appearing, in what order, and that interaction is being simulated. The plan is the contract.
180	
181	## Audio planning
182	
183	Choose the music direction in the plan. Leave exact SFX file selection and exact timestamps to Hyperframes during composition, because SFX should match the actual visual implementation.
184	
185	Default posture: include audio. Pick a music bed and a few tasteful SFX unless the user passed `--no-music` / `--no-sfx`, the assets are missing, or silence is explicitly part of the concept.
186	
187	For each scene, note the intended audio role and likely audio-coupled opportunities:
188	
189	Format: `Audio-coupled idea: type the hook with subtle key ticks if Hyperframes uses a typing animation.`
190	
191	For audio-reactive visuals, say what should respond and how restrained it should be. Example: `Audio-reactive treatment: subtle; use music RMS/bass to make the hero glow and product card presence breathe, not to add waveform bars.`
192	
193	Do not require exact SFX filenames in `brag-plan.md` unless the user explicitly requested a specific sound or the mapping is unavoidable. Prefer moment types and intent.
194	
195	Hyperframes has creative freedom to choose exact files, density, and timestamps that make the video feel smooth and professional.
196	
197	Do not over-specify audio if the tone asks for restraint. For `yc-parody` or `deadpan`, use fewer and quieter cues, but prefer polished restraint over no audio.
198	
199	## Music cue guidance
200	
201	Beat/cue sync is available for any track now (see `audio.md` → "Beat and cue sources"): bundled tracks have precomputed presets; custom tracks get cues at composition time via `analyze_music_cues.py` (rich, needs Python) or `npx hyperframes beats` (simple, zero-dep). When the plan chooses music, add a compact `Music cue guidance` section to `brag-plan.md`:
202	
203	- The track and, if a preset exists, its tempo.
204	- 1-3 strong-cue timestamps to target for major visual moments — from the preset if bundled, otherwise note "to be detected at composition time."
205	- Beat-grid windows for any sequential reveals in the storyboard.
206	- A restraint note when the tone is deadpan, yc-parody, or otherwise quiet.

209	
210	If SFX are enabled, note likely sound opportunities but leave exact filenames to Hyperframes. Hyperframes should use the skill's `sfx-analysis.md` during composition.
211	
212	## Handoff posture
213	
214	- Good: "Recreate the swipe card with Thunder's profile and hay tags."
215	- Good: "Use the source site's amber/dark palette and serif headline feel."
216	- Good: "The stat reveal should feel like a deadpan startup metric slide."
217	- Avoid: "Use a GSAP timeline with this selector and this easing."
218	- Avoid: "Use this exact HTML structure."
219	- Avoid: "Load this specific runtime URL."
220	
221	## Transition vocabulary
222	
223	Match transitions to tone:
224	
225	| Tone | Preferred transitions |
226	|---|---|
227	| `default` | Crossfade, clean wipe |
228	| `polished` | Soft crossfade, slide |
229	| `yc-parody` | Hard cut, minimal |
230	| `chaotic` | Hard cut, flash, zoom |
231	| `deadpan` | Slow crossfade, long hold |
232	| `cinematic` | Dramatic wipe, crossfade |
233	| `app-store` | Slide, smooth wipe |

153	## Beat sync (when a cue source is available)
154	
155	Get a cue source first (see `audio.md` → "Beat and cue sources"): a bundled preset, `analyze_music_cues.py` on any track (needs Python; run via `uv`), or `npx hyperframes beats` (no Python; needs Hyperframes ≥ 0.6.99). The rich sources (preset / `analyze_music_cues.py`) give two arrays; `hyperframes beats` gives one.
156	
157	- **`strongCues`** — high-intensity beats (drops, swells, accents). Use for **major moments**: scene transitions, hero reveals, match payoff, logo landing. Lock 1–3 per video. With `hyperframes beats` (no `strongCues`), take the highest-`strength` beats instead.
158	- **`beats`** — the full beat grid. Use to **snap small sequential events** into the music's pulse: cards arriving one by one, stats popping in, sequenced SFX hits.
159	
160	### How to implement
161	
162	**Major moments (strong cues):**
163	1. Load the cue source: the preset/analysis JSON (`strongCues` + `beats`), or the beat-grid JSON that `hyperframes beats` writes (a plain beat list; see the current hyperframes-cli skill for its location).
164	2. Pick 1–3 strong timestamps near a planned major visual moment — `strongCues`, or the highest-`strength` beats.
165	3. Shift the reveal's start time to land within ±0.15s of the cue.
166	4. Mark it: `// beat-locked: 5.80s`
167	
168	**Sequential events (beats):**
169	1. Decide how many sequential items there are (e.g. 3 stats, 4 profile cards).
170	2. Find the nearest beat to your intended start time for the first item.
171	3. Use consecutive beats from that point for each subsequent item — snap each within ±0.10s of a beat timestamp.
172	4. Mark it: `// beat-grid: stat 1 at 12.65s, stat 2 at 13.17s, stat 3 at 13.70s`
173	
174	**Readable text vs the beat grid:** if the sequential items are text the viewer reads (stat labels, list rows, callouts) and the beats are close (under ~0.6s apart at fast tempos), do not reveal a new line on every beat — it outruns reading (this rushed the bicycles spec rows). Snap to every other beat, or reveal them quickly and hold the full set on screen afterward. Non-text accents (glows, dots, ticks) may still hit every beat. See the reading-time floor in `step-2-plan.md`.
175	
176	This gives you two layers of musicality: the big moments land on the strongest hits, and the small events tick along with the pulse.
177	
178	Do not force every tween onto a beat — readability and scene pacing come first. If snapping a tween to a beat hurts copy legibility or the product story, use the natural timing instead.
179	
180	If SFX are enabled, also pass `<skill-dir>/assets/sfx/sfx-analysis.md` as selection guidance. Prefer low high-frequency-risk files for repeated or polished moments. SFX on sequential events should fire at the same timestamp as the visual — the sound and motion land together.

199	## Self-review checklist
200	
201	Before moving to delivery, verify:
202	
203	- [ ] `<output-dir>/composition-brief.md` exists.
204	- [ ] The brief clearly identifies the exact product moments to show.
205	- [ ] The composition uses the current Hyperframes workflow, not a hardcoded `/brag` template.
206	- [ ] Music file is copied into `<output-dir>/composition/assets/music/`.
207	- [ ] At least one visual element subtly reacts to the music (audio-reactive treatment present), or extraction failure is documented.
208	- [ ] At least 1 major tween is beat-locked to a strong cue (a `strongCue`, or the highest-`strength` beat from `hyperframes beats`) within ±0.15s, marked `// beat-locked` (or natural timing was chosen for readability).
209	- [ ] Sequential events (cards, stats, list items) snap to consecutive `beats[]` timestamps (±0.10s), marked `// beat-grid` (or natural timing was chosen for readability).
210	- [ ] The composition shows at least one real UI, copy, or visual element from the project.
211	- [ ] Every factual claim on screen is grounded in the project (see below).
212	- [ ] Total duration is 15-25 seconds.
213	- [ ] Hyperframes check passes, or any blocker is documented for the user.
214	
215	### Grounding factual claims
216	
217	`hyperframes check` audits structure. It has no opinion on copy, so a scene
218	can read "Ships 10x faster" — a sentence nobody in the project ever wrote —
219	and still come back clean. Read the composition once with this question in
220	mind, because nothing else will ask it.
221	
222	The line is between what the video *asserts* and how it *says* it.
223	
224	**Must be grounded.** Names, numbers, capabilities, feature claims, quotes,
225	anything presented as the product's own copy. If a line states something about
226	the product, that something has to appear in the project — its files, its
227	README, its UI, its actual output. Re-cased, trimmed or split across elements
228	is fine; invented is not. "Streamline your workflow" fails not because it is
229	generic but because it is a claim the project never makes.
230	
231	**Free to invent.** Tone, framing, jokes, hooks, transitions, connective
232	narration. "Here's the part nobody asked for" is made up and welcome — it is
233	the craft, and it asserts nothing about the product.
234	
235	When a line you want is not grounded, the fix is usually to quote what the
236	project does say, which is almost always stranger and better than the
237	invented version.

1	# Step 4: Validate, render, and deliver
2	
3	## Validate
4	
5	```bash
6	cd <output-dir>/composition
7	npx hyperframes check   # brag's single pre-render gate — fix every error it reports
8	```
9	
10	Fix all errors. `check` is brag's single pre-render gate — run it and fix everything it reports, including WCAG contrast failures (they gate as errors, not warnings). Each contrast finding carries a suggested compliant color, so apply it or adjust within the palette family and re-run `check` — most fixes need no screenshot. There is no per-element contrast escape hatch for real text; the only bypass is `check --no-contrast`, which skips the entire WCAG pass (all-or-nothing), not a way to accept one borderline element. For exact contrast thresholds, layout escape hatches, and reporting details, follow the current hyperframes-cli `check` guidance. `check`'s layout pass backstops the "keep all text readable" creative law — fix any reported overflow.
11	
12	Read the contrast coverage too. If the composition has visible DOM text but reports `0/0 text checks` or zero elements checked, its contrast is unverified even if `check` prints "passed". Inspect `npx hyperframes check --json` and the sampled frames to find what was skipped. If unsupported `oklch()` colors are the cause, convert the affected colors to equivalent sRGB hex or `rgb()` values, verify that the palette still matches, and rerun `check`. Continue only when the expected text is actually audited and the contrast findings are resolved; `--no-contrast` does not satisfy this gate.
13	
14	For a visual gut-check before rendering, optionally capture key frames:
15	
16	```bash
17	npx hyperframes snapshot   # PNG key frames
18	```
19	
20	## Preview
21	
22	```bash
23	npx hyperframes preview
24	```
25	
26	Tell the user the preview is running and give them the localhost URL. Invite them to check it before rendering.
27	
28	If the user approves or asks to render:
29	
30	## Render
31	
32	```bash
33	npx hyperframes render --output ../brag.mp4
34	```
35	
36	This outputs to `<output-dir>/brag.mp4` (one level up from the composition directory).
37	
38	For a faster iteration render:
39	```bash
40	npx hyperframes render --quality draft --output ../brag.mp4
41	```
42	
43	For final delivery:
44	```bash
45	npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output ../brag.mp4
46	```
47	
48	## Pick the poster frame
49	
50	The poster is the still shown before the video plays — the first thing anyone sees when it's idle or unplayed. Don't leave it to the raw first frame or an arbitrary timestamp; those land on fades, mid-transitions, blank intro backgrounds, or half-rendered text.
51	
52	You built this composition, so you already know its strongest moment and exactly when it lands — the hook line, the hero reveal, or the final logo. Pick that beat at a **settled** point: text fully animated in, before it exits (the storyboard timings tell you the safe window). Then extract that one frame full-res with ffmpeg. From `<output-dir>/composition`:
53	
54	```bash
55	# use the timestamp of your strongest settled beat, e.g. 3.2s
56	ffmpeg -ss 3.2 -i ../brag.mp4 -frames:v 1 -q:v 2 ../brag.jpg
57	```
58	
59	Aim for a frame that's postable on its own (the "show the thing" law — any frozen frame should be shareable). If the pulled frame lands on a transition or mid-animation, nudge the timestamp a few tenths of a second and re-extract.
60	
61	### Bake the poster as frame 0
62	
63	A bare `.mp4` has no `poster` attribute — every player and platform picks its own idle thumbnail, and almost all of them grab **frame 0**. Slack, Twitter/X, and Discord regenerate thumbnails server-side and ignore embedded cover-art metadata, so the *only* reliable way to control the idle image everywhere is to make frame 0 *be* the poster.
64	
65	Replace **only** the first frame's pixels with `brag.jpg`, leaving every other frame and all timing untouched — same duration, same frame count, audio copied through. At 30fps the poster shows for 1/30s before the intro rolls, so it's imperceptible on playback but it's what every thumbnail grabber sees. From `<output-dir>`:
66	
67	```bash
68	ffmpeg -y -i brag.mp4 -i brag.jpg \
69	  -filter_complex "[0:v][1:v]overlay=0:0:enable='eq(n,0)'[v]" \
70	  -map "[v]" -map "0:a?" -c:v libx264 -crf 18 -preset slow -pix_fmt yuv420p \
71	  -c:a copy -movflags +faststart brag.poster.mp4 \
72	  && mv brag.poster.mp4 brag.mp4
73	```
74	
75	The poster (`brag.jpg`) matches the video's dimensions because it was pulled from the same render, so the overlay lines up exactly. Keep `brag.jpg` alongside — it's the custom-thumbnail asset for platforms that accept an upload (Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Facebook, and the LinkedIn post editor) and the `poster="brag.jpg"` image for any `<video>` that embeds the brag (a gallery card, the user's site).
76	
77	## Write share copy
78	
79	Write `<output-dir>/share-copy.txt`.
80	
81	The share copy should be:
82	- One to three sentences max
83	- Postable as-is to Twitter/X, LinkedIn, or Discord
84	- Specific to the project — no generic "excited to share" language
85	- Tone-matched to the brag video
86	
87	`share-copy.txt` is the canonical single caption. Do not put multi-platform variants, long launch notes, or Product Hunt copy in this file.
88	
89	If variants are useful, write them to a separate optional file:
90	
91	```text
92	<output-dir>/share-copy-variants.md
93	```
94	
95	### Share copy by tone
96	
97	**`default`:**
98	```
99	Made [App Name]. It's [what it does, in the project's own absurd terms].
100	[The best line from the product.]
101	```
102	
103	**`polished`:**
104	```
105	Introducing [App Name]: [clean one-liner from the site].
106	Built with [stack if notable].
107	```
108	
109	**`yc-parody`:**
110	```
111	We built [App Name] to solve [problem stated completely seriously].
112	[Deadpan feature or stat.]
113	```
114	
115	**`chaotic`:**
116	```
117	[ALL CAPS CLAIM].
118	[App Name] is [wildly overstated description].
119	Link below.
120	```
121	
122	**`deadpan`:**
123	```
124	I made [App Name].
125	It [what it does].
126	```
127	
128	**`cinematic`:**
129	```
130	[App Name].
131	[Tagline from the site, verbatim or lightly adapted.]
132	```
133	
134	**`app-store`:**
135	```
136	[App Name] is now live.
137	[Feature 1], [Feature 2], and [Feature 3] — all in one place.
138	```
139	
140	### Example: Taxi for Taxis
141	
142	```
143	Every day, taxis carry us. But who carries the taxis?
144	Taxi for Taxis: the ride-hailing app for ride-hailing assets.
145	Available in 12 metros.
146	```

1	# Audio reference
2	
3	All SFX are CC0 (Kenney.nl, public domain). The bundled music is CC BY 4.0 by Sascha Ende (ende.app); see `assets/music/README.md`. Music and SFX should be used by default unless the user passes `--no-music`, `--no-sfx`, the required assets are missing, or the plan explicitly chooses silence as the strongest creative move.
4	
5	Bias toward a smooth, professional result: one tasteful music bed plus a small number of well-timed SFX usually feels better than silence.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## Audio-reactive visuals
10	
11	When music is present, prefer a subtle audio-reactive treatment unless the tone asks for stillness or deadpan restraint. This does not mean beat detection. It means Hyperframes can pre-extract per-frame audio data and use RMS/frequency-band energy to modulate existing visual elements.
12	
13	Good uses:
14	- Hero glow or sky warmth breathes slightly with RMS
15	- Product card, phone, or metric panel gains subtle presence on bass
16	- Title, quote, or logo gets a soft treble glow on stronger musical moments
17	- Background depth, vignette, or light layer gently swells with the bed
18	
19	Avoid:
20	- Waveform displays, equalizer bars, musical notes, or generic visualizer graphics
21	- Strobing, heavy pulsing, or text scaling that hurts readability
22	- Treating audio-reactivity as a substitute for good scene timing
23	- Claiming exact beat/BPM sync unless a real beat detector is available
24	
25	Suggested plan notation:
26	```
27	Audio-reactive treatment: subtle; use music RMS/bass to make the hero glow and product card presence breathe. No waveform/equalizer visuals.
28	```
29	
30	Hyperframes implementation note: follow the audio-reactive guidance owned by the `media-use` skill (`audio/references/captions/motion.md`; let that skill locate its own files), to extract per-frame audio data and sample it synchronously inside the composition timeline. That file is written for captions: use its build-time audio modulation pattern on brand elements (glow, halo, card presence), not on caption groups. The extraction helper (`audio/scripts/extract-audio-data.py`) ships with that skill — `/brag` does not provide it, so don't hardcode a path to it.
31

36	All paths below are relative to `<skill-dir>`, this skill's own directory (see "Skill directory" in `SKILL.md`). It differs by install method, so resolve it rather than assuming `~/.claude/skills/brag/`.

38	SFX live under `<skill-dir>/assets/sfx/{casino,impact,interface,ui}/`, and the individual keypress set under `<skill-dir>/assets/sfx/keyboard/`.

40	Music lives at `<skill-dir>/assets/music/`.

80	## SFX library — approved files

166	
167	## Tone → SFX energy
168	
169	| Tone | Energy | Approach |
170	|---|---|---|
171	| `default` | Moderate | 3-5 SFX at key moments. `interface/click` or `interface/drop_*` for pop-ins, `impactBell_heavy_000` for success, `impactSoft_medium` for reveals. |
172	| `polished` | Minimal but present | 2-3 very subtle SFX. `interface/bong_001` for a soft accent. `interface/drop_001` for a gentle reveal. Nothing aggressive. |
173	| `yc-parody` | Sparse but present | 2-3 restrained cues. One dry reveal hit (`impactSoft_medium`), one UI/card accent, one logo payoff if it fits. |
174	| `chaotic` | Dense | SFX on every beat, sometimes stacked. Mix `impact/impactPunch_heavy`, `interface/glitch_002`, `casino/dice-throw`, `impact/impactMetal_heavy`. |
175	| `deadpan` | Very sparse | Prefer one quiet music bed plus 1-2 dry cues. Full silence only when the plan explicitly says silence is the joke. |
176	| `cinematic` | 2-3 big ones | `impactBell_heavy_000` or `_004` for the hero moment. `impactSoft_medium` for the reveal. `impactBell_heavy_003` for the outro. |
177	| `app-store` | Consistent light layer | `interface/drop_*` or `interface/click_*` per feature card. `impactBell_heavy_000` on outro. All at 0.65-0.75 volume. |
178	
179	---
180	
181	## Moment → sound heuristics
182	
183	Use these as examples for Hyperframes, not a fixed recipe. Sound should reinforce the edit, not call attention to itself.
184	
185	| Moment type | Good sound families | Notes |
186	|---|---|---|
187	| Sequential cards/items opening | `casino/card-slide-*`, `casino/card-place-*`, `casino/card-fan-*`, `interface/drop_*` | Match the gesture. A card stack uses card sounds; a soft product grid can use drop sounds. For dense sequences, accent the first, last, or rhythmically important items only. |
188	| Big reveal / payoff | `impact/impactBell_heavy_000`, `_003`, or `_004`, `impact/impactSoft_medium_*`, `interface/bong_001` | One short announcement-style cue when the reveal lands. Keep it brief. |
189	| Text popping / typed copy | `keyboard/keypress-*.wav` (randomized), `interface/drop_*` | For per-character typing animations, pick a random file from `keyboard/` for each character. For soft label pop-ins, use `drop_001` or `drop_002`. Thin out or skip when copy is dense. |
190	| Simulated user action | `interface/click_*`, `interface/select_008`, `interface/switch_*`, `ui/mouseclick1`, `ui/switch*` | Use interaction sounds when the video shows a cursor, tap, button, toggle, swipe, or selection. Match the visible action. |
191	| Success / completion | `impact/impactBell_heavy_000`, `_003`, or `_004`, `casino/chips-collide-*` | Positive accent for approvals, matches, metrics, completed flows, or final CTAs. |
192	| Chaotic or comedic beat | `interface/glitch_002`, `interface/glitch_004`, `interface/error_005–006`, `impact/impactPunch_heavy_*`, `casino/dice-throw-*` | Reserve louder or weirder cues for tones that can handle them. |
193	
194	When in doubt, pick fewer cues with better timing. Prefer a coherent sonic palette for the whole video over a grab bag of cute sounds.
195	
196	---
197	
198	## Timing rules
199	
200	These rules apply when Hyperframes is implementing the composition and the motion timings are known:
201	
202	- Align SFX to the **start** of the animation, not the end
203	- Entry pop: 0.0–0.1s before the element's first visible frame
204	- Transition: at the transition start time
205	- Success ding: at the moment the metric/stat is fully visible
206	- For staggered elements: usually accent the first, final, or strongest beat; only score every item when that rhythm is intentional and still feels clean
207	
208	Composition notation:
209	```
210	Scene 2 — Reveal — 3s
211	  "Horse Tinder" scales in at 0.3s  →  SFX: impact/impactSoft_medium_001 at 0.2s
212	  Tagline fades up at 0.8s          →  (no SFX, let the reveal carry)
213	  Transition at 3.0s                →  SFX: interface/drop_001 at 2.9s
214	```
215	
216	---
217	
218	## Music
219	
220	### Available tracks
221	
222	All tracks are "Happy Beats / Business Moves" by ende.app. Upbeat, clean, corporate-adjacent. Good across multiple tones.
223	
224	| Filename | Duration | Character | Best for |
225	|---|---|---|---|
226	| `happy-beats-business-moves-vol-1-by-ende-dot-app.mp3` | 2:44 | Full upbeat track, most energetic | `default`, `app-store` |
227	| `happy-beats-business-moves-vol-9-by-ende-dot-app.mp3` | 1:54 | Mid-energy, slightly more laid-back | `default`, `yc-parody` |
228	| `happy-beats-business-moves-vol-10-by-ende-dot-app.mp3` | 1:00 | Compact loop, punchy | `default`, `chaotic` |
229	| `happy-beats-business-moves-vol-11-by-ende-dot-app.mp3` | 1:28 | Warm and business-y | `yc-parody`, `app-store` |
230	| `happy-beats-business-moves-vol-12-by-ende-dot-app.mp3` | 1:58 | Steady and clean | `polished`, `cinematic` |
231	
232	For `deadpan` tone: prefer vol-12 at very low volume (0.12-0.18). Skip music only if the plan explicitly chooses silence.
233	
234	### In a composition
235	
236	After copying files (see Asset paths above), reference them with relative paths from `composition/`:
237	
238	```html
239	<audio id="bg-music" data-start="0" data-duration="[total]" data-track-index="10" data-volume="0.35" src="assets/music/happy-beats-business-moves-vol-1-by-ende-dot-app.mp3"></audio>
240	```
241	
242	Volume: 0.3-0.4 for normal music beds. Use 0.12-0.22 for deadpan or very restrained parody. Never above 0.5. SFX at 0.55-0.85, with softer values for polished/deadpan.
243	
244	If the music file doesn't exist, skip it and notify the user after rendering.
245	
246	### Beat and cue sources
247	
248	Beat sync needs a cue source. Three are available — use the richest one the environment supports. Beat sync now works on **any** track, not just bundled ones. The two any-track methods (2 and 3) have orthogonal requirements — option 2 needs Python, option 3 needs a recent Hyperframes — so when one is unavailable the other usually covers it.
249	
250	1. **Bundled track → precomputed preset (richest, instant, no deps).** The bundled tracks ship with cue metadata. Read the matching markdown summary, and pass the JSON path in `composition-brief.md`:
251	
252	```text
253	<skill-dir>/assets/music/cues/<track-stem>.music-cues.md
254	<skill-dir>/assets/music/cues/<track-stem>.music-cues.json
255	```
256	
257	2. **Any track → extended analysis (richest for custom tracks; needs Python, any Hyperframes version).** For a custom track — or to refresh a bundled one — run `analyze_music_cues.py` on the audio file. It produces the same rich cue JSON/Markdown for any track. Run it via `uv`, which auto-provisions the deps (`librosa`, `numpy`, `scipy`, `soundfile`) from `<skill-dir>/scripts/pyproject.toml` — no manual `pip install` needed:
258	
259	```bash
260	uv run --project <skill-dir>/scripts \
261	  python <skill-dir>/scripts/analyze_music_cues.py <track>.mp3 \
262	  --output-json <output-dir>/composition/assets/music/cues/<stem>.music-cues.json \
263	  --output-md  <output-dir>/composition/assets/music/cues/<stem>.music-cues.md
264	```
265	
266	This is the fallback when `hyperframes beats` (option 3) is unavailable — e.g. an older pinned Hyperframes. If neither `uv` nor the Python deps are available, use option 3 instead.
267	
268	3. **Any track → `hyperframes beats` (simple, no Python; needs Hyperframes ≥ 0.6.99).** After the music is wired into the composition, run:
269	
270	```bash
271	npx hyperframes beats <output-dir>/composition
272	```
273	
274	It writes a per-track beat file: a beat grid with per-beat timing and a normalized `strength` (0-1), but no separate `strongCues` array — so derive "strong" beats by taking the highest-`strength` ones. (See the current hyperframes-cli `beats` guidance for the exact output path.) `beats` was added in Hyperframes 0.6.99; on an older pinned install it won't exist — fall back to option 2 (the script), or to the `unavailable` note below.
275	
276	The preset and `analyze_music_cues.py` share the rich schema:
277	
278	- `duration`, `tempo`
279	- `beats`: beat-grid points with `time` and normalized `intensity`
280	- `strongCues`: highest-value landing moments with `time`, `intensity`, and `kind` (`strong_beat` / `onset_peak`)
281	- `scoring`: feature and normalization metadata
282	
283	`hyperframes beats` is the simpler floor: a plain beat grid with a per-beat strength, no strong-cue array.
284	
285	Planning rules (apply to whichever source you have):
286	
287	- Use cue metadata to bias timing, not control it.
288	- Major reveals may move toward strong cues within about `±0.15s`.
289	- Smaller entrances may align to nearby beat points within about `±0.10s`.
290	- Use 1-3 strong cue locks per 15-25s video.
291	- Ignore cues when they harm copy readability, scene pacing, or the product story.
292	- For deadpan or restraint-heavy tones, cues should be rare, quiet, or saved for the final logo.
293	
294	Cue/beat metadata is not a substitute for Hyperframes audio-reactive visuals: it helps with beat/swell timing; audio-reactive data helps subtle visual properties breathe with the music.
295	
296	If no source is available (no preset, no Python deps, and `hyperframes beats` not run), write:
297	
298	```text
299	Music cue guidance: unavailable; continue without beat/cue sync.
300	```
301	
302	### Adding SFX elements
303	
304	Put the music bed on a low track and give each overlapping SFX its own ascending track-index (e.g. music at 10, SFX from 11 up). Never share a track-index between overlapping audio.
305	
306	```html
307	<audio id="sfx-1" data-start="0.2" data-duration="1" data-track-index="11" data-volume="0.80" src="assets/sfx/interface/drop_001.ogg"></audio>
308	```
309	
310	Wire each `<audio>` clip per the current hyperframes Data Attributes + Video/Audio contract (`data-track-index`, `data-volume`, `data-start`, `data-duration`). `/brag` owns only the volume policy above and the track-allocation convention; Hyperframes owns the clip schema.

1	# Tone reference
2	
3	Seven tones. Each changes scripting energy, pacing, typography personality, and transition style.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## `default`
8	
9	**Energy:** Playful, clean, postable. The product gets to be funny on its own terms.
10	
11	**Voice:** First person plural. Warm. Direct. No corporate language.
12	
13	**Typography:** Mixed case. Comfortable weight. Let words breathe.
14	
15	**Pacing:** 4-5 scenes. Each scene 3-5 seconds. Comfortable rhythm.
16	
17	**Hook style:** A simple question or observation that sets up the reveal.
18	```
19	Dating apps were built for humans.
20	Obvious mistake.
21	```
22	
23	**Highlight style:** Short punchy phrases. One idea per scene.
24	```
25	Swipe through eligible horses near your pasture.
26	```
27	
28	**Outro style:** The product name, then a tagline. Light punchline.
29	```
30	Horse Tinder.
31	Find your perfect stablemate.
32	```
33	
34	**Transitions:** Crossfade or clean slide.
35	
36	**When to use:** Most absurd consumer apps. Projects that have personality without trying too hard.
37	
38	---
39	
40	## `polished`
41	
42	**Energy:** Serious, elegant. Uses restraint as the creative choice.
43	
44	**Voice:** Third person or no voice. The product speaks for itself.
45	
46	**Typography:** Mixed case. Light-to-medium weight. Generous letter-spacing. Nothing aggressive.
47	
48	**Pacing:** 3-4 scenes. Each scene 4-6 seconds. Confidence through slow reveals.
49	
50	**Hook style:** A single strong image or the product name at full scale.
51	
52	**Highlight style:** One feature per scene. No bullets. No lists.
53	```
54	Wing certification
55	upon completion.
56	```
57	
58	**Outro style:** Product name. Tagline. Silence.
59	
60	**Transitions:** Slow crossfade (0.6-0.8s).
61	
62	**When to use:** Projects that aren't jokes. Products that want to feel premium. Anytime the user says "clean" or "elegant."
63	
64	---
65	
66	## `yc-parody`
67	
68	**Energy:** Deadpan startup launch energy. The joke is how seriously it's delivered.
69	
70	**Voice:** Serious. Matter-of-fact. No winking. The absurdity comes from the product, not the tone.
71	
72	**Typography:** Sentence case. Heavy weight or medium weight. Courier-adjacent for data points. No decoration.
73	
74	**Pacing:** 4-5 scenes. Structured. Each scene makes one claim.
75	
76	**Hook style:** The problem, stated completely seriously.
77	```
78	Every day, taxis carry us.
79	But who carries the taxis?
80	```
81	
82	**Highlight style:** Feature or metric stated as fact.
83	```
84	Available in 12 metros.
85	99.1% fleet uptime.
86	```
87	
88	**Outro style:** Product name. The tagline. A URL that implies legitimacy.
89	```
90	Taxi for Taxis
91	The ride-hailing app for ride-hailing assets.
92	taxifortaxis.com
93	```
94	
95	**Transitions:** Hard cut or minimal crossfade (0.2s).
96	
97	**When to use:** Any recursive or absurd concept that benefits from being played straight. "Psychologists for Chatbots", "Taxi for Taxis", "Briefcase for Baby."
98	
99	---
100	
101	## `chaotic`
102	
103	**Energy:** Fast, loud, unhinged. The video is the joke.
104	
105	**Voice:** Aggressive. SHORT WORDS. CAPS. Metric dumps. Exclamation marks optional but not mandatory — confidence is louder.
106	
107	**Typography:** ALL CAPS. Heavy weight. Slightly oversized. Some words tilted. Some words larger than expected.
108	
109	**Pacing:** 6-8 scenes. Some scenes under 2 seconds. Never more than 4 seconds per scene.
110	
111	**Hook style:** Something that shouldn't exist, stated at full volume.
112	```
113	TRANSPORTATION WAS TOO CALM.
114	```
115	
116	**Highlight style:** Rapid-fire. One word or one number per beat.
117	```
118	8,400 BOARS
119	3 MINUTE ETA
120	TUSKS-FIRST PICKUP
121	```
122	
123	**Outro style:** The name slams in. Tagline hits. Cut to black.
124	```
125	UBER FOR WILD BOARS
126	On-demand chaos, now with routing.
127	```
128	
129	**Transitions:** Hard cut. Flash cut (brief white/black frame). Zoom cut (scale 1.2→1.0 on entrance).
130	
131	**When to use:** Chaotic concepts, logistics parodies, anything that can be played as a hype reel. "Uber for Wild Boars", anything with urgency or speed.
132	
133	---
134	
135	## `deadpan`
136	
137	**Energy:** Calm. Dry. The joke is that nothing registers as unusual.
138	
139	**Voice:** Minimal. One observation. Then the product. That's it.
140	
141	**Typography:** Mixed case. Large. Sparse. Lots of empty space. One thought at a time.
142	
143	**Pacing:** 3-4 scenes. Long holds. 4-7 seconds per scene. The pace is the joke.
144	
145	**Hook style:** A quiet observation. No setup. No punchline yet.
146	```
147	I used to fear the sky.
148	```
149	
150	**Highlight style:** One sentence per scene. No bullets. No excitement.
151	```
152	Now I fear birds, weather, and gravity.
153	```
154	
155	**Outro style:** The product name. Nothing else. Maybe a very small tagline. Long hold on empty space.
156	```
157	Fish Flight School.
158	```
159	
160	**Transitions:** Very slow crossfade (0.8-1.0s). Or long hold before the next scene.
161	
162	**When to use:** Projects that have a quote as the strongest thing on the site. "Psychologists for Chatbots" testimonial-forward approach. Anything where restraint makes the joke land harder.
163	
164	---
165	
166	## `cinematic`
167	
168	**Energy:** Dramatic. Trailer-scale. The product is being treated like a blockbuster.
169	
170	**Voice:** Epic. Short declarative sentences. Each one lands before the next begins.
171	
172	**Typography:** ALL CAPS or heavy mixed case. Full-bleed scenes. Large type. Significant scale.
173	
174	**Pacing:** 4-5 scenes. 3-5 seconds each. Dramatic reveals, not quick cuts.
175	
176	**Hook style:** A sweeping statement about the world, stated seriously.
177	```
178	For too long,
179	fish were told to stay underwater.
180	```
181	
182	**Highlight style:** The product's capabilities stated like superpowers.
183	```
184	Thermal identification.
185	Cloud navigation.
186	Emergency splash landing protocols.
187	```
188	
189	**Outro style:** Product name slams in full-screen. Tagline. Music swell implied.
190	```
191	FISH FLIGHT SCHOOL
192	The sky was never the limit.
193	```
194	
195	**Transitions:** Dramatic wipe or slow crossfade with scale (scene enters at 0.95, reaches 1.0).
196	
197	**When to use:** Anything with natural epic quality. "Fish Flight School" maps perfectly. Anything involving scale, nature, or grand claims.
198	
199	---
200	
201	## `app-store`
202	
203	**Energy:** Clean. Professional. Feature-forward. The product is real (even when it's not).
204	
205	**Voice:** Feature-benefit. Third person. Present tense.
206	
207	**Typography:** Title case. Medium weight. Clean, readable. No aggression.
208	
209	**Pacing:** 4-6 scenes. Each scene: product name or feature name, then 1-2 supporting details.
210	
211	**Hook style:** Product name + tagline, clean.
212	```
213	Psychologists for Chatbots.
214	Because even helpful assistants need help.
215	```
216	
217	**Highlight style:** Feature card structure. Name + brief description.
218	```
219	Prompt Trauma Processing
220	Identify and resolve harmful conversation patterns.
221	```
222	
223	**Outro style:** CTA-style. Call to action or download prompt.
224	```
225	Available now.
226	All chatbot models welcome.
227	```
228	
229	**Transitions:** Clean slide or wipe (0.35-0.45s). Nothing dramatic.
230	
231	**When to use:** Products that benefit from being taken seriously as a product, even if absurd. Good for anything B2B-parody or therapy/wellness adjacent.

# The Watchmaker's Bench

A browser app where anyone learns why a mechanical watch runs fast or slow by diagnosing and regulating a live, simulated movement, read through a timegrapher (rate in s/day, amplitude in degrees, beat error in ms).

`watchmaker_brief.md` is the source of truth for concept and scope. `CLAUDE.md` carries decisions and working rules. `SPIKE.md` records the escapement spike that preceded this build.

## Development

Requires Node 22 or newer.

```sh
npm ci            # install (no browser downloads; Playwright browsers are fetched only by the verify-render skill)
npm run dev       # Vite dev server
npm run build     # tsc --noEmit, then vite build → dist/
npm run preview   # serve dist/ locally
npm test          # vitest run (sim core)
```

## Deployment

Static site on Cloudflare Pages. Pushing to `main` redeploys production; every other branch gets a preview URL. Agents deploy with the `deploy` skill (`.claude/skills/deploy/`): preview any branch any time, promote to `main` only on Akash's go-ahead. See `docs/hosting.md`, "Deploy process".

Production URL: https://watchmakers-bench.pages.dev

    "typescript": "^5.6.0",
    "vite": "^6.0.0",
    "vitest": "^3.0.0",
    "playwright": "^1.50.0"
  }
}

/** Diagnosis puzzles: a bundled faulty watch, a symptom, a hidden cause, a completion rule. */
import type { WatchSettings, WatchSpec, WatchReading } from "../core/watch";
import type { Reading } from "../core/timegrapher/analyze";
import { TIRED_MAINSPRING } from "../core/oscillator/amplitude";

export interface Puzzle {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  symptom: string;
  goal: string;
  /** Hidden faults added to the user's settings. */
  faults: Partial<WatchSettings>;
  /** Hidden changes to the calibre itself. */
  specOverride?: (w: WatchSpec) => WatchSpec;
  /** Band the readings must stay inside (what the instrument shows, plus the physics), and for how long (sim seconds). */
  band: (r: WatchReading, tg: Reading | null) => boolean;
  holdSeconds: number;
  explanation: string;
  /** Which controls this puzzle shows, in display order, left to right. State of wind is a condition
   *  of the watch, not a repair, so every puzzle shows it. */
  controls: ("regulator" | "beat" | "wind" | "screws" | "position" | "poise")[];
  /** For puzzles with no knob fix: a two-choice question ends them instead of a band. */
  question?: { prompt: string; choices: string[]; correct: number; whyCorrect: string };
}

export const PUZZLES: Puzzle[] = [
  {
    id: "runs-fast",
    title: "Runs fast",
    symptom: "The owner says it gains about 40 seconds a day.",
    goal: "Slide <b>Regulator index</b> toward S (slow) until <b>rate</b> reads between −5 and +5 s/day. Hold it there for 60 seconds of ticks.",
    faults: { regulatorIndex: 1.2 },
    band: (r, tg) => r.running && !!tg && Math.abs(tg.rateSecondsPerDay) <= 5,
    holdSeconds: 60,
    explanation:
      "The regulator index had been pushed toward F. Its two pins pinch the hairspring nearer its end, so a shorter length of spring does the work; a shorter spring is stiffer and swings the balance back a little quicker on every beat. Moving the index toward S frees more spring, and the beats slow back to true time.",
    controls: ["regulator", "wind"],
  },
  {
    id: "out-of-beat",
    title: "Out of beat",
    symptom: "The ticking sounds uneven: tick-tock, tick-tock, like a limp. It keeps good time.",
    goal: "Slide <b>Beat adjustment</b> until the two lines on the screen become one and <b>beat error</b> reads under 0.5 ms. Hold it there for 60 seconds of ticks.",
    faults: { beatOffsetDeg: 6 },
    band: (r, tg) => r.running && !!tg && tg.beatErrorMs < 0.5,
    holdSeconds: 60,
    explanation:
      "The hairspring held the balance at rest slightly off centre, so the balance reached the fork early on one side of its swing and late on the other. Tick and tock were unequal: that gap is the beat error. Turning the stud carrier (the beat adjustment) moves the rest position back to centre, and the two lines on the screen merge.",
    controls: ["beat", "wind"],
  },
  {
    id: "afternoon-slump",
    title: "Afternoon slump",
    symptom: "Fine in the morning, gains by evening. Regulating it only moves the problem.",
    goal: "Slide <b>State of wind</b> from 0 h toward 40 h and watch <b>amplitude</b> and <b>rate</b> change together. Then answer the question below. No slider fixes this one.",
    faults: {},
    specOverride: (w) => ({ ...w, mainspring: TIRED_MAINSPRING }),
    band: () => false,
    holdSeconds: Infinity,
    question: {
      prompt: "You have watched it run down. What do you tell the owner?",
      choices: ["Move the regulator toward S to cancel the evening gain.", "The mainspring is tired. Regulating only shifts the error around the day. Fit a new mainspring."],
      correct: 1,
      whyCorrect: "Right. The regulator moves the whole day's rate up or down together; it cannot flatten the curve. The evening gain comes from the swing shrinking, and only the mainspring's push sets the swing.",
    },
    explanation:
      "This mainspring is tired: its push fades 40 % over a day instead of 15 %, so the balance's swing shrinks by evening. In a flat-hairspring watch like this one a smaller swing runs faster, because the regulator pins touch the spring differently; the escapement alone would make it lose, but the pins win. Some errors are physics, not adjustment: the fix is a new mainspring.",
    controls: ["wind", "regulator"],
  },
  {
    id: "position-error",
    title: "Position error",
    symptom: "Keeps good time lying on the nightstand, loses on the wrist.",
    goal: "Set <b>Position</b> to each crown position and compare <b>rate</b> with dial up. Find the heavy spot on the balance rim, then slide <b>Poising</b> to remove weight there until crown up and crown down each read within 3 s/day of dial up.",
    faults: { unbalance: 10e-11, heavySpotDeg: 0 },
    // Research 04: a well-milled balance has a residual of about 1.5 µg·cm = 1.5e-11 kg·m.
    band: (r) => r.running && r.netUnbalance <= 1.5e-11,
    holdSeconds: 60,
    explanation:
      "One spot on the balance rim is heavier than the rest: the balance is out of poise. Lying flat, gravity pulls along the axis and the heavy spot does nothing; standing up, gravity tugs it on every swing. A heavy spot at the bottom makes the watch lose above about 220° of amplitude and gain below it, so the error even changes between a fresh wind and the evening.",
    controls: ["position", "poise", "wind"],
  },
];
/** Named states for the verify-render skill. Each sets puzzle, settings and animation phase. */
import type { WatchSettings } from "../core/watch";
import type { Phase } from "../core/escapement/kinematics";
import type { Highlight } from "../view/movement";

export interface NamedState {
  describe: string;
  puzzle: string | null;
  settings: Partial<WatchSettings>;
  /** Freeze the animation at the middle of this escapement phase on this beat (0 entry, 1 exit). */
  freeze?: { phase: Phase; beat: 0 | 1; frac?: number };
  /** Highlight the part a control acts on, as while that slider is being dragged. */
  highlight?: Highlight;
  /** Show the hidden heavy spot (as after solving puzzle 4). */
  reveal?: boolean;
  /** Simulated seconds of ticks to accumulate before the shot. */
  simSeconds: number;
  expect: { phase?: Phase; rateWithin?: [number, number]; amplitudeWithin?: [number, number]; beatErrorBelow?: number; running?: boolean };
}

hyperframes v0.9.44 — Create and render HTML video compositions

Usage:  hyperframes <command> [options]

Getting Started:
  init               Scaffold a new composition project
  add                Install a block or component from the registry
  capture            Capture a website for video production
  catalog            Browse and install blocks and components
  preview            Start the studio for previewing compositions
  present            Open a slideshow deck in presenter mode (with audience sync)
  share              Share a rendered video for review
  publish            Upload a project to a stable URL (private by default)
  render             Render a composition to MP4 or WebM
  open               Open a project in the HyperFrames desktop app
  catch-up           See what was done in the desktop app since you last looked

Project:
  lint               Validate a composition for common mistakes
  check              Run lint, runtime validation, and layout inspection as one gate
  validate           Runtime-validate a composition in headless Chrome (JS errors, missing assets, contrast)
  beats              Detect beats in the music track and write beats/<audio>.json
  audio              Measure where sounds land: onsets, hits, loudness, silence, in film time
  inspect            Inspect rendered visual layout across the timeline
  keyframes          Inspect keyframes and render onion-shot diagnostics
  snapshot           Capture key frames as PNG screenshots for visual verification
  media-treatment    Discover, apply, or clear deterministic media treatments on media elements
  normalize-audio    Match one authored audio clip's loudness to another using integrated LUFS
  grade-compare      Render candidate color grades onto a reference frame as one labeled comparison PNG
  compare            Render composition variants into one labeled comparison sheet
  diff               Score a render or a project against the original video, frame by frame
  measure            Measure a video file: clock, cuts, events, frames, motion, crops, boxes, eases, look
  reverse            Open a reverse-any-video run: note it with HeyGen, then probe the video
  billing            Open the HyperFrames plans or credits page and wait until it is done
  templates          Pull a style template into this project (HyperFrames Pro)
  info               Print project metadata
  compositions       List all compositions in a project
  timeline           Print the project's tracks and clips
  history            List, undo and restore the project's recorded changes
  docs               View inline documentation in the terminal

Tooling:
  benchmark          Render with preset fps/quality/worker configs and compare speed and file size
  browser            Manage the Chrome browser used for rendering
  doctor             Check system dependencies and environment
  clean              Find and remove what HyperFrames left on disk
  upgrade            Check for updates and show upgrade instructions
  update             Check the CLI and the skills for updates in one call, and install them

Deploy:
  cloud              Render compositions on HeyGen's cloud (no local Chrome/ffmpeg)
  lambda             Deploy and drive distributed renders on AWS Lambda
  cloudrun           Deploy and drive distributed renders on Google Cloud Run

AI & Integrations:
  skills             Install HyperFrames and GSAP skills for AI coding tools
  transcribe         Transcribe audio/video to word-level timestamps, or import an existing transcript
  models             List or download on-device models (models list, models install parakeet)
  tts                Generate speech audio from text using a local AI model (Kokoro-82M)
  remove-background  Remove background from a video or image to produce transparent media

=== data-attributes

Data Attributes

Core attributes for controlling element timing and behavior.

Timing

  • data-start="0" — Start time in seconds
  • data-duration="5" — Duration in seconds
  • data-track-index="0" — Studio timeline lane, display only. The render never reads it, and it does not control paint order (use CSS z-index) or prevent overlap. Optional.

Media

  • data-media-start="2" — Media playback offset / trim point (seconds)
  • data-volume="0.8" — Audio/video gain. 1 is 0 dB, 0 is silence, and values above 1 boost up to 3.98 (+12 dB). For ducking and shaped envelopes use the data-automation volume lane (/media-use → references/mixing.md)
  • data-fade-in="0.5" / data-fade-out="1" — Clip-edge fades (seconds): linear gain ramps anchored to the clip's start and end, multiplied on top of data-volume and any volume lane
  • data-has-audio="true" — Keeps the file's sound on this clip (the default for footage with sound). Silent footage uses muted instead.

Composition

  • data-composition-id="root" — Unique ID for composition wrapper (required)
  • data-width="1920" — Composition width in pixels
  • data-height="1080" — Composition height in pixels
  • data-composition-src="./intro.html" — Nested composition source

Element Visibility

Add class="clip" to timed elements. The runtime keys visibility off data-start, not this class, but the shared .clip rule is what gives a scene its full-frame box and Studio treats it as an edit hint.

=== compositions

Compositions

A composition is an HTML document that defines a video timeline.

Structure

Every composition needs a root element with data-composition-id:

<div id="root" data-composition-id="root" data-width="1920" data-height="1080">
  <!-- Elements go here -->
</div>

Nested Compositions

Embed one composition inside another:

<div data-composition-src="./intro.html" data-start="0" data-duration="5"></div>

Listing Compositions

Use npx hyperframes compositions to see all compositions in a project.

Variables

Two attributes with different shapes and different jobs:

  • **data-composition-variables** on the <html> root — a JSON **array of declarations** ({id, type, label, default} per entry). Defines the schema: which variables exist, what type they are, and what defaults to use when no override is provided.
  • **data-variable-values** on a sub-comp host element — a JSON **object keyed by variable id** ({"title":"Pro","price":"$29"}). Carries per-instance overrides for that one mount of the sub-composition.

They aren't redundant — one is "what variables does this composition have?" and the other is "what values should this particular embed use?" Inside any composition script, window.__hyperframes.getVariables() returns the merged result. Layering, lowest to highest precedence:

1. Declared defaults from data-composition-variables
2. Per-instance overrides from the host's data-variable-values (sub-comp embeds only)
3. CLI overrides from npx hyperframes render --variables '{...}' (top-level renders only)

<!-- compositions/card.html -->
<html data-composition-variables='[
  {"id":"title","type":"string","label":"Title","default":"Hello"},
  {"id":"color","type":"color","label":"Color","default":"#111827"}
]'>
  <body>
    <div data-composition-id="card" data-width="1920" data-height="1080">
      <h1 class="title"></h1>
      <script>
        const { title, color } = window.__hyperframes.getVariables();
        document.querySelector(".title").textContent = title;
        document.querySelector(".title").style.color = color;
      </script>
    </div>
  </body>
</html>

<!-- index.html — embed twice with different per-instance values -->
<div data-composition-id="card-pro" data-composition-src="compositions/card.html"
     data-variable-values='{"title":"Pro","color":"#ff4d4f"}'></div>
<div data-composition-id="card-enterprise" data-composition-src="compositions/card.html"
     data-variable-values='{"title":"Enterprise","color":"#22c55e"}'></div>

The runtime layers data-variable-values over the sub-comp's declared defaults on a per-instance basis. The same getVariables() call works at the top level too — the CLI flag --variables provides the override, declared defaults fall through for missing keys.

=== gsap

GSAP Animation

HyperFrames uses GSAP for animation. Timelines are paused and controlled by the runtime.

Setup

<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/gsap@3/dist/gsap.min.js"></script>
<script>
  const tl = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
  tl.to("#title", { opacity: 1, duration: 0.5 }, 0);
  window.__timelines = window.__timelines || {};
  window.__timelines["root"] = tl;
</script>

Key Rules

  • Always create timelines with { paused: true }
  • Register timelines on window.__timelines with the composition ID as key
  • Position parameter (3rd arg) sets absolute time: tl.to(el, vars, 1.5)
  • Supported methods: set, to, from, fromTo

Supported Properties

opacity, x, y, scale, scaleX, scaleY, rotation, width, height, visibility

=== audio

Audio

Audio plays from <audio> and <video> elements, timed like any other clip.

Timing and trim

  • data-start and data-duration — when the clip plays and for how long, in seconds
  • data-media-start — where in the file playback begins (trim point)

Level

  • data-volume — gain. 1 is 0 dB, 0 is silence, values above 1 boost up to 3.98 (+12 dB)
  • data-fade-in and data-fade-out — linear fades at the clip edges, in seconds
  • data-has-audio="true" — keeps a video's own sound (the default for footage with sound); use muted on silent footage
  • data-automation volume lane — ducking and shaped envelopes, multiplied on top of the above

Related

  • hyperframes docs data-attributes — every timing and media attribute
  • hyperframes transcribe — word timestamps for captions; see hyperframes docs transcribe

=== rendering

Rendering

Render compositions to MP4 (or another --format) with npx hyperframes render.

Local Mode (default)

Uses Puppeteer (bundled Chromium) + system FFmpeg. Fast for iteration.
Requires: FFmpeg installed (brew install ffmpeg or apt install ffmpeg).

Docker Mode (--docker)

Deterministic output with exact Chrome version and fonts. For production.
Requires: Docker installed and running.

Options

  • -f, --fps — 1-240 or a rational such as 30000/1001 (default: root data-fps, else 30)
  • -q, --quality — draft, looks, delivery, or standard/high (default: looks)
  • --format — Output format: mp4, webm, mov, gif, png-sequence, or hls (default: mp4). MOV and WebM keep transparency; png-sequence writes RGBA frames to a directory; hls writes a VOD playlist directory (H.264/AAC, SDR only, no GPU encoding)
  • --gif-loop — GIF loop count, 0 for infinite (0-65535). Only used with --format gif
  • -w, --workers — Parallel workers 1-24 or auto; higher values are capped at 24 (default: auto)
  • --crf — Override encoder CRF (mutually exclusive with --video-bitrate)
  • --video-bitrate — Target video bitrate such as 10M (mutually exclusive with --crf)
  • --keyframe-interval — MP4 only: a keyframe at least every N seconds (default: encoder's choice)
  • --max-bitrate — MP4 only: peak video bitrate cap such as 8M, kept alongside the quality target (default: uncapped)
  • --buffer-size — MP4 only: buffer for --max-bitrate, such as 16M (default: twice --max-bitrate)
  • --vp9-cpu-used — WebM VP9 speed/quality tradeoff (-8 to 8, default: 4). Higher values encode faster with larger output / quality tradeoff.
  • --video-frame-format — Source video frame extraction format: auto, jpg, or png (default: auto). Use png for UI recordings, screen captures, and color-sensitive source videos.
  • --chroma-subsampling — MP4 chroma: 420 or 444 (default: 420). 444 keeps full-resolution colour for thin coloured text and UI (yuv444p, lossless PNG capture, slower). SDR MP4 with the software encoder only; many players cannot decode 4:4:4.
  • --gpu — Use GPU encoding (NVENC, VideoToolbox, AMF, VAAPI, QSV)
  • --browser-gpu / --no-browser-gpu — Force host GPU or software (SwiftShader) for Chrome/WebGL capture. Default for local renders is auto — probe WebGL availability on first launch and fall back to software if no GPU is reachable. Docker mode always uses software.
  • -o, --output — Custom output path

Tips

  • Use draft quality for fast previews during development
  • Local renders auto-detect GPU on first launch; use --browser-gpu to force hardware (errors if no GPU) or --no-browser-gpu to force SwiftShader
  • Use --gpu when a local render also benefits from hardware FFmpeg encoding
  • Use --video-frame-format png when source videos contain saturated UI colors that should avoid JPEG extraction
  • Use --chroma-subsampling 444 for text- and UI-heavy MP4 masters; keep the default for files you publish directly
  • Use npx hyperframes benchmark to find optimal settings
  • 4 workers is usually the sweet spot for most compositions

=== troubleshooting

Troubleshooting

"No composition found"

Your directory needs an index.html. Run npx hyperframes init to create one.

"FFmpeg not found"

Local rendering requires FFmpeg. Install it:

  • macOS: brew install ffmpeg
  • Ubuntu: sudo apt install ffmpeg
  • Windows: Download from https://ffmpeg.org/download.html

Lint errors

Run npx hyperframes lint to check for common issues:

  • Missing data-composition-id on root element
  • Missing class="clip" on timed elements
  • Overlapping timelines or invalid data attributes

Preview not updating

Make sure you're editing the index.html in the project directory. The preview server watches for file changes and auto-reloads.

Render looks different from preview

Use --docker mode for deterministic output. Local renders may differ due to font availability and Chrome version.

"hot" : ""}" transform="translate(${half - 24},${-bottom - 18})"><circle cx="0" cy="0" r="6"/>${adj.view.gravity === "into-page" ? `<line x1="-4" y1="-4" x2="4" y2="4"/><line x1="-4" y1="4" x2="4" y2="-4"/>` : `<circle cx="0" cy="0" r="1.4" fill="currentColor"/>`}<text x="10" y="4">g</text></g>`) : "";
